evidence.quote: Persistent storage can retain delivered data after a process stops or an instance's running life ends. The service lifecycle and deletion policy still matter. Amazon EBS volumes can outlive an EC2 instance, but its delete-on-termination setting can remove a volume when the instance terminates. Inspect the actual setting instead of assuming it survives.

The operation's scope matters: syncing a file does not necessarily persist its directory entry; Linux may also require syncing the containing directory. Follow the supported procedure for the operation and storage stack instead of treating one call as a universal recipe.

mechanisms.reason: Volume-and-layers and safe-provisioning identify what changes at attach, format and mount. Write-completion traces volatile buffers to the device, awaiting completion and errors; shared-access explains stale independent caches and conflicting disk-structure writes. Snapshots-and-recovery connects partial delivered state to application recovery and correct restore handling. Both diagrams are accurate: the first is explicitly one database-on-files path, not a universal path, and the second depicts independent host caches sharing an uncoordinated device.

evidence.quote: A filesystem organizes blocks into files, directories and metadata. A database using those files adds records, queries and transaction rules. These are layers with different responsibilities: a database can use block storage without the volume becoming a database.

An ordinary single-host filesystem assumes it controls its disk structures. Two independent mounts can each cache an old view and make conflicting updates, overwriting metadata or data. Attachment can succeed while concurrent writing is unsafe. AWS explicitly warns that ordinary XFS and EXT4 filesystems are not designed for simultaneous access from multiple servers.

coherence.reason: All eight card objectives are built in order: addressed volume/layers, safe setup, persistence/deletion/failure scope, write completion, coordination, snapshot recovery, performance and interface selection. Prerequisites are introduced before use, and examples serve mechanisms without requiring a recurring narrative.

evidence.quote: A volume restored from a snapshot can already contain a filesystem and valuable data. Formatting it overwrites filesystem structures and can destroy access to that data. Successful attachment gives no reason to run a format operation automatically.

A snapshot preserves a volume's state at a point in time. EBS snapshots capture data written to the volume, excluding bytes still in application or operating-system caches. During an application update, the stored state may contain only some related writes.

decisions.reason: The lesson explains when not to format, not to assume survival from persistence, not to equate multi-attach with shared files, not to trust snapshot success as application recovery and not to buy volume speed before finding host/workload limits. Workload-fit then justifies block/file/object/database choices while retaining operator responsibilities. These are usable decisions grounded in the stated mechanisms.

evidence.quote: If the requirement is simply shared files and directories, consider a shared file service. Shared block access needs a filesystem or application expressly designed to coordinate it. Verify both provider attachment support and the software's coordination requirements; enabling a volume option does not supply those rules.
If the host or another part of the application is the bottleneck, buying more volume performance may not reduce application latency. Find where the time goes before changing the setting.

Choosing block storage leaves filesystem or database management, safe attachment, deletion settings, capacity, performance and tested recovery to the system's operators. Choose by access pattern, sharing and recovery needs, not just by the familiarity of a disk.

clarity.reason: Provision/attach/format/mount, AZ, fsync, snapshot/crash recovery and four performance metrics are defined plainly. evidence.quote: Formatting creates a filesystem. Mounting makes that filesystem accessible at a location in the host's directory tree. For file use, format only the verified empty intended volume; mount a suitable existing filesystem without formatting it again.

Capacity measures how much data fits. IOPS counts input/output operations per second. Throughput measures bytes transferred per second. I/O latency is the time one operation takes to complete. More capacity alone does not guarantee faster access.

sourceChecks.claim: Comparison page block section describes logical block addresses and selected block access; file section supplies names and directory organization. Supports distinction of interface layers, not automatic database semantics.

EBS setup page says attachment exposes a block device, requires identification and filesystem inspection, and warns that creating a filesystem over a restored existing one overwrites data. Supports inspect-before-format and mount-existing guidance.
EBS Features directly documents same-AZ attachment/replication, independent volume lifetime and delete-on-termination. No zone-outage or deletion recovery promise follows from component redundancy.

Linux man-pages fsync primary manual describes file data/metadata flushing, blocking until device completion, error return and separate containing-directory synchronization. Additional primary https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.fsync confirms application buffered-file flush must precede fsync.

EBS Multi-Attach explicitly warns XFS/EXT4 are not designed for simultaneous access and requires coordinated filesystem/application behavior and write ordering. Volume access alone is not metadata or transaction coordination.

EBS snapshot creation directly documents point-in-time written-volume data, exclusion of application/OS caches, asynchronous pending state and paused writes preparation. Safe restore formatting follows the setup page; retention and application validation are reasoned recovery requirements, not a guarantee from job success.
EBS IO characteristics defines operations, queue/latency, request-size/throughput relationship and instance bandwidth limits; supports workload-based diagnosis and no universal speed ranking.

EBS volumes documents disk-like devices, system/database use and frequent updates; additional source https://aws.amazon.com/compare/the-difference-between-block-file-object-storage/ verifies file/object interface contrasts. Remaining operator obligations are established by earlier cards, not all stated on the volume overview.
